newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan election picture shapes up as LDP comeback.
newsitem.headline: Japan election picture shapes up as LDP comeback.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party -- trounced at the polls in 1993 -- is poised to bounce back in Sunday's general election, with some political analysts even forecasting a possible landslide.
All opinion polls have the LDP, Japan's largest party, as favourites to either win a slim majority or form the next government with defections from other parties.
If forecasts hold up, it would be a remarkable comeback by the LDP which has steadily built itself up since the 1993 disaster.
It clawed its way into a coalition government one year after the setback and is now just one step away from again dominating Japanese politics with a win in the first election since 1993.

Polls show the LDP is benefiting from emergence of the Democratic Party, which is taking votes from the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), said Takayoshi Miyagawa of the Centre for Political Public Relations, a think tank.
"It's not that the LDP is doing any better than expected, only that Shinshinto is doing far worse because the undecided and anti-LDP votes appear to be going to the Democrats," he said.

The Democratic Party was formed only last month. It boasts as one of its leaders Health Minister Naoto Kan, who has won national hero status this year by uncovering his ministry's role in hushing up a scandal over HIV-tainted blood products.
Miyagawa said he has upgraded his former projection that the LDP would secure about 260 seats in the 500-seat Lower House to a forecast that "even 290-300 seats are possible".

Such a forecast is a dramatic turnaround from what was expected when official campaigning started 10 days ago. At that time, the LDP and Shinshinto were neck-and-neck, with neither expected to win a majority.

The higher projections for the LDP reflect expectations that as many as 30 of Sunday's winners outside the LDP -- independents and members of Shinshinto and smaller opposition groups -- will join the LDP after the election, Miyagawa said.
"The key, if not sole, factors in the rosy scenario for the LDP are the Democrats' emergence and every other group's desire to be part of the ruling party," Miyagawa said.
LDP leaders have carefully laid out a welcome mat for the return of any prodigal sons who defected from the LDP when its unbroken 38-year rule ended in 1993, he said.

The LDP is also in the best position to take advantage of a new electoral system, in which 300 seats will be contested in first-past-the-post constituencies -- a change that favours large parties with strong local organisation.
The other 200 seats will be decided by proportional representation, determined by party strength.
Reacting to the rosy projections, LDP Secretary-General Koichi Kato has told party supporters not to let down their guard or let turnout fall.
"Staying away from polls thinking the LDP is home safe is tantamount to giving half a vote to the opposition," Kato told supporters at party headquarters earlier this week.
Surveys show voters may stay away from polling stations in record numbers. Forecasts say the turnout may be below 60 percent. The postwar record low turnout is 1993's 67.26 percent.
The weather forecast for Sunday is fine, another factor which analysts say favours the LDP, because it will enable the party's strong nationwide organisation to get out the vote.
The LDP ruled Japan from 1955 to 1993. After a brief period out of power, it came back as the dominant partner in a coalition government from mid-1994.
The biggest losers are expected to be the LDP's coalition partners for the past two years in the outgoing government, the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake, polls say.
